title: Divisibility Tests for Divisors Sharing Factors with 10
description: Extends the osculator divisibility test to divisors that share factors with 10 (d = 2, 4, 5, 8, 25, etc.). If d | 10^k, then d | n iff d | (n mod 10^k) — check the last k digits. For composite divisors like 6, 12, 15: factor into coprime parts, test the power-of-2/5 part by last digits, and the coprime part by osculator.

meta.assumptions: None. All theorems fully proved using Mathlib's GCD and divisibility API.

overview.historicalContext: The parent proof handles divisors coprime to 10 via the osculator method (multiplying by a 'magic constant' and truncating). OQ-02 asks: what about divisors like 2, 4, 5, 8, 25 that share factors with 10? The answer combines two tests: last-k-digits for the power-of-10 factor, osculator for the coprime factor.
overview.problemStatement: Can the divisibility truncation method be extended to divisors sharing factors with 10?
overview.text: Yes. Any divisor d can be written as d = a·b where a | 10^k and gcd(b, 10) = 1. Then d | n iff a | (last k digits of n) AND b | n (using osculator). This combines the last-k-digits test with the osculator method.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. Prove last_k_digits_test: d | 10^k implies d | n ↔ d | (n mod 10^k).
2. Prove coprime factoring: gcd(a,b) = 1 implies ab | n ↔ a | n ∧ b | n.
3. Combine: test power-of-10 factor by last digits, coprime factor by osculator.
4. Demonstrate with concrete examples (div by 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 15, 25, 125).
keyInsights: If d | 10^k, then d | n iff d divides the last k digits of n
Coprime factoring: ab | n iff a | n ∧ b | n (when gcd(a,b) = 1)
Combined test splits any divisor into a power-of-10 part (last digits) and coprime part (osculator)
Examples: div by 4 checks last 2 digits; div by 12 = 4·3 checks last 2 digits AND digit sum

conclusion.text: The divisibility truncation method extends to all divisors by combining last-k-digits testing with the osculator method. This fully answers OQ-02.
conclusion.implications: Any divisibility test can now be decomposed into a digit-check and an osculator step.
